summary: DANE lets a domain's administrators publish in DNS which keys or certificates their TLS servers use, using the TLSA record. This reduces dependence on third-party certificate authorities and requires changes in client software but not server software.

plainLanguage.summary: DANE TLSA lets a domain publish which certificate or public key a TLS service should present. A client checks the DNSSEC-protected record and compares it with the server's certificate before accepting the connection.

questions: what are the tlsa certificate usages
where are tlsa records stored in dns
subtitle: How DNSSEC-protected TLSA records associate a domain and service with a certificate or key.

tldr.problem: TLS clients traditionally rely on public certification authorities, and any trusted authority can issue certificates for any domain name.
tldr.mechanism: A domain publishes a TLSA record in DNSSEC-protected DNS. The record identifies a certificate or public key association for a particular host, transport, and port; a client validates DNSSEC and compares the association with the server's certificate.
tldr.outcome: DANE TLSA lets domain administrators specify certificate associations without changing TLS server software, but requires client support and DNSSEC. RFC 6698 has been updated by RFC 7218, RFC 7671, and RFC 8749.

today: RFC 6698 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2012. It has been updated by RFC 7218, RFC 7671, and RFC 8749; read those updates alongside it.

sections.title: Why DANE Uses DNSSEC for TLS
sections.content:
TLS uses certificates to associate a service name with a public key. In the public certificate-authority model described by the RFC, any trusted CA can issue a certificate for any domain, so a compromised or untrustworthy CA can undermine that association.

DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) lets a domain administrator publish certificate information in DNS, with DNSSEC protecting the record's authenticity and integrity. This RFC defines DANE TLSA for TLS and DTLS using PKIX certificates. It does not define how a client performs DNSSEC validation.
sections.plainLanguage: DANE lets a domain publish which certificate information its TLS service expects clients to see. DNSSEC helps clients check that the published information has not been changed.

sections.title: The TLSA Record Fields
sections.content:
A TLSA record contains three one-octet fields followed by certificate association data: certificate usage, selector, and matching type. The selector chooses the full certificate or its SubjectPublicKeyInfo. The matching type chooses exact data, a SHA-256 hash, or a SHA-512 hash.

The certificate usage says how the association applies: constrain the CA, constrain the service certificate, assert a trust anchor, or match a domain-issued certificate without PKIX path validation. In zone-file form, the three fields are unsigned 8-bit integers and the association data is hexadecimal.
sections.plainLanguage: Three small fields tell a client how to interpret the certificate association. They choose the certificate role, which certificate content to inspect, and whether to compare the content directly or by hash.

sections.title: The Four Certificate Usages
sections.content:
Usage 0 requires a matching CA certificate to appear in a valid PKIX path. Usage 1 requires the server's end-entity certificate to match and pass PKIX validation. Usage 2 says which certificate must serve as the trust anchor when validating the end-entity certificate.

Usage 3 requires the server's end-entity certificate to match the association but does not test PKIX validation. This allows a domain administrator to issue a certificate without using a third-party CA. These usage values are defined for PKIX certificates in DER encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: The usage value determines whether the record constrains a CA, the service certificate, or the trust anchor. The domain-issued usage checks for a certificate match without requiring PKIX validation.

sections.title: The DNS Name for a TLSA Record
sections.content:
Unless another protocol specifies a different name, a TLSA record is stored under a name built from the service port, transport, and TLS server name. The first label is an underscore followed by the decimal port without leading zeros. The second is an underscore followed by the transport name, such as tcp, udp, or sctp.

For example, the RFC gives _443._tcp.www.example.com for a TLS service on port 443 at www.example.com. Including the port and transport lets one host have distinct associations for different services.
sections.plainLanguage: The client looks up the record at a DNS name that includes the service's port and transport. This keeps the association specific to that service on the host.

sections.title: How a TLS Client Uses the Record
sections.content:
A client retrieves TLSA records and uses their DNSSEC validation state. A secure record set must be used unless local policy prohibits an association. A bogus result means TLS must not start, or an existing handshake must be aborted. Indeterminate or insecure data cannot be used as a TLSA association.

The client ignores associations it cannot understand, that are malformed, or that use algorithms too weak for its policy. If no usable association remains, TLS proceeds normally. If usable associations exist, the client compares them with the server's end-entity certificate and must abort the handshake if none match. The TLS session must use the port and transport named in the lookup.
sections.plainLanguage: The client first checks whether DNSSEC validated the record. A bogus result stops the connection; usable associations must match the server's certificate or the client ends the handshake.

sections.title: Publishing a Replacement Certificate
sections.content:
A secure TLSA record set is used by conforming clients, so a misconfigured record can prevent them from accessing the service. The RFC does not provide a gradual transition mechanism. Administrators should account for how clients build certificate chains when choosing between matching the full certificate and matching SubjectPublicKeyInfo.

For certificate rollover, the RFC describes a pre-publish sequence: add the new TLSA record alongside the old one, wait for the new data to propagate and for the old record's TTL to expire, switch the server to the new certificate, then remove the old record.
sections.plainLanguage: Publish the new certificate association before changing the server certificate. After the new record has propagated and old cached data has expired, switch certificates and then remove the old record.

sections.title: Trust and DNS Security Risks
sections.content:
TLSA security depends on DNSSEC and on protecting changes to TLSA data at least as strongly as changes to address records. A compromised DNS signing key can alter associations within its zone, but DNSSEC keys are limited to signing data in their zone. TLSA associations are also limited to the name, protocol, and port used for the query.

Usage 2 can treat a certificate as a trust anchor, which may override revocation and policy restrictions that would otherwise apply. The RFC also warns that a TLS-inspecting proxy that substitutes its own certificate will not match the TLSA association. If clients cache lookup results, they must observe DNS TTL values.
sections.plainLanguage: DANE is only as trustworthy as the DNSSEC validation and the process for changing DNS records. A trust-anchor association has extra consequences because it can bypass some certificate checks.

items.label: CA constraint
items.desc: A CA certificate must appear in a valid PKIX path.

items.label: Service certificate constraint
items.desc: The end-entity certificate must match and pass PKIX validation.

items.label: Trust anchor assertion
items.desc: The matching certificate is used as the trust anchor.

items.label: Domain-issued certificate
items.desc: The end-entity certificate must match; PKIX validation is not tested.
